chapters.title: Probability
chapters.what: Probability measures how often an outcome occurs in the long run. Counting outcomes gives the binomial and Poisson laws; random sampling (Monte Carlo) estimates any probability or area.
chapters.looks: Bars of the exact probabilities with the histogram of simulated samples on top; in 3D a joint distribution of two variables as a surface with its samples.
chapters.change: ▶ grows the number of samples: the histogram settles onto the exact bars (the law of large numbers).
chapters.use: Radioactivity counting, quality control, reliability of components, risk, Monte Carlo simulation.
misc: Independent events multiply; mutually exclusive events add.
A long run of heads does not make tails 'due'.

examples.title: Counting α particles: a Poisson law
examples.world: Rutherford and Geiger counted scintillations in 1/8-minute intervals: a mean of 3.87 per interval, Poisson-distributed.

examples.title: Ten coin tosses: 5 or 6 heads
examples.world: Sampling inspection and opinion polls are binomial experiments.

examples.title: Monte Carlo: π from random points
examples.world: The Monte Carlo method was named for this kind of random sampling (Metropolis & Ulam 1949).

examples.title: Monte Carlo in 3D: the volume of a ball
examples.world: High-dimensional integrals (physics, finance) are done this way; the error falls like 1/√n in any dimension.

chapters.title: Probability distributions
chapters.what: A distribution tells how a random quantity spreads: its density (or mass) function, its cumulative function, its mean and variance. A few families describe most data.
chapters.looks: The density with the probability of an interval shaded; in 3D a correlated pair of normals.
chapters.change: Change the shape parameter of a Weibull from 1 to 3.5: exponential failures become wear-out failures.
chapters.use: Tolerances, wind energy, particle sizes, reliability, signal noise.
misc: A density can exceed 1; probabilities cannot.
Mean ± σ covers 68% only for the normal.

examples.title: Heights are roughly normal
examples.world: Adult heights: μ = 175 cm, σ = 7 cm; 68% lie within one σ.

examples.title: Wind speeds follow a Weibull law
examples.world: Scale 8 m/s, shape 2 (Rayleigh): 22% of the time below a turbine's 4 m/s cut-in speed.

examples.title: Particle sizes are log-normal
examples.world: Aerosols, grains and incomes: the logarithm is normal.

examples.title: Waiting times between random events are exponential
examples.world: Calls to a help desk at 0.5 per minute: 63% of gaps are shorter than 2 minutes.

examples.title: Defective parts in a batch of 50
examples.world: With a 2% defect rate, 92% of batches have at most two defects.

examples.title: Small samples: Student's t

chapters.title: Statistics: estimation, regression, the central limit theorem
chapters.what: Statistics infers from data: estimates with their uncertainty, lines and surfaces that best fit (least squares), and the central limit theorem that makes averages normal.
chapters.looks: Data with the fitted curve and residuals (2D), a fitted plane through a cloud of points (3D), and histograms of sums turning into a bell curve.
chapters.change: Raise the polynomial degree: the fit passes closer to every point but predicts worse (over-fitting).
chapters.use: Calibration curves, experimental design, quality control, machine learning.
misc: R² close to 1 does not prove the model is right.
The CLT needs finite variance — and enough terms if the terms are skewed.

examples.world: The total of ten dice is already bell-shaped.

chapters.title: Uncertainty quantification
chapters.what: Every measured input carries an uncertainty; a computed result inherits one. The GUM's linear rule adds sensitivity-weighted uncertainties in quadrature; Monte Carlo propagates the whole distribution.
chapters.looks: The histogram of Monte Carlo results against the linear-rule normal (2D); the response surface with the sampled inputs on it (3D).
chapters.change: Make the input uncertainty large in a nonlinear formula: the Monte Carlo result becomes skewed and wider than the linear rule says.
chapters.use: Calibration certificates, engineering safety margins, measurement standards, simulation credibility.
misc: Uncertainties add in quadrature only if the inputs are independent.
The linear rule fails when f is strongly curved over ±u.

examples.title: Electric power P = V I
g from a pendulum: g = 4π² L/T²
A ratio with large uncertainties: the linear rule fails
examples.world: x/y with 10 ± 1 and 2 ± 0.5: the Monte Carlo spread is wider and skewed.

examples.title: Monte Carlo error falls as 1/√n
examples.world: ∫₀¹ e^{−x²} dx by random points: 100× more points, 10× smaller error.

examples.title: Errors that accumulate like a random walk
examples.world: Dead-reckoning navigation drifts like √N steps.

chapters.title: Numerical foundations: floating point, error, conditioning
chapters.what: Computers store numbers with about 16 significant digits (machine epsilon 2.2×10⁻¹⁶). Every numerical method trades truncation error (from approximating) against round-off error (from storing).
chapters.looks: The V-shaped error of a difference quotient on log–log axes; interpolation curves wildly overshooting at the ends.
chapters.change: Switch from equally spaced to Chebyshev nodes: the interpolation error collapses.
chapters.use: Every simulation code; financial calculations; control of rounding in instruments.
misc: A smaller step is not always more accurate.
Adding more interpolation points on an even grid can make things worse (Runge).

examples.title: The best step for a forward difference is about 10⁻⁸
examples.world: Truncation ∝ h, round-off ∝ ε/h: they balance at h ≈ √ε.

examples.title: A central difference does better: h ≈ 10⁻⁵
examples.world: Truncation ∝ h², so the balance moves to h ≈ ε^{1/3}.

examples.title: Second derivatives: cancellation bites harder
examples.world: The error of (f(x+h) − 2f(x) + f(x−h))/h² grows like ε/h² for small h.

examples.title: Runge's phenomenon on equally spaced nodes
examples.world: Degree-10 interpolation of 1/(1 + 25x²) overshoots near ±1 (max error 1.92).

examples.title: Chebyshev nodes cure it
examples.world: The same degree on Chebyshev nodes: max error 0.109.

examples.title: Explicit Euler on a stiff decay blows up
examples.world: hλ = −2.5 lies outside Euler's stability disk.

chapters.title: Root finding
chapters.what: Solving f(x) = 0 by iteration: bisection halves a bracket (slow, certain); Newton follows tangents (fast, needs a good start); the secant method needs no derivative.
chapters.looks: Tangent lines and brackets closing in on the root (2D); a staircase of log|f| falling with each iteration (3D).
chapters.change: Start Newton far away or near a flat spot: it can overshoot or cycle; bisection never fails if the signs differ.
chapters.use: Square roots in calculators, Kepler's equation for orbits, pipe friction factors, equations of state.
misc: Newton's convergence is quadratic only near a simple root.
Bisection needs a sign change.

examples.title: Newton's own example: x³ − 2x − 5 = 0
examples.world: Newton (1669) and Raphson (1690) solved this cubic; root 2.0945515.

examples.title: Bisection: slow but certain
examples.world: Thirty halvings of [2, 3] pin the root to 10⁻⁹.

examples.title: How a calculator finds √2
examples.world: Newton on x² − 2 doubles the correct digits each step.

examples.title: Kepler's equation E − e sin E = M
examples.world: Every orbit calculation solves it; e = 0.5, M = 1 rad gives E = 1.4987.

examples.title: The Colebrook friction factor

examples.title: The secant method needs no derivative
examples.world: Kepler's equation again: order ≈ 1.6 instead of 2.

chapters.title: Numerical differentiation
chapters.what: Derivatives from function values: forward differences are first-order accurate, central differences second-order; the step h must balance truncation against round-off.
chapters.looks: Log–log error curves with slopes 1 or 2 on the right (truncation) and −1 on the left (round-off); in 3D the same error over x.
chapters.change: Add high-frequency noise to f: derivatives of measured data become useless for small h.
chapters.use: Velocities and accelerations from positions, sensitivity analysis, Jacobians for Newton solvers.
misc: Differentiation amplifies noise; integration smooths it.
A central difference is exact for quadratics (up to rounding).

examples.world: The workhorse of finite-difference codes.

examples.title: Forward difference: first order
examples.world: Cheap (one extra evaluation) but its error falls only like h.

examples.title: Second derivative (curvature, acceleration)
examples.world: Accelerations from GPS positions need the second difference.

examples.title: Noisy data: the derivative drowns
examples.world: A 10⁻⁶ ripple at 1000 rad⁻¹ swamps the difference quotient below h ≈ 10⁻³.

examples.title: Velocity of a falling ball from its position
examples.world: h(t) = 100 − 4.905 t²: the central difference is exact for a quadratic.

chapters.title: Numerical integration
chapters.what: Quadrature replaces an integral by a weighted sum of function values: trapezoid (error ∝ h²), Simpson (∝ h⁴), Gauss (exact for high-degree polynomials), Monte Carlo (∝ 1/√n in any dimension).
chapters.looks: The panels under the curve and, in 3D, the disks or slabs they become.
chapters.change: Double n: the trapezoid error drops ×4, Simpson's ×16.
chapters.use: Areas and volumes from measurements, energies from force records, ship hydrostatics, finite elements.
misc: Simpson needs an even number of intervals.
Sharp features need more points where they are, not everywhere.

examples.world: 8 panels: 1.9742 instead of 2.

examples.title: Simpson's rule on the same integral
examples.world: 8 panels: error 1.7 × 10⁻⁵.

chapters.title: Numerical ODE solvers and stability
chapters.what: A solver is stable for y′ = λy only if hλ lies in its stability region |R(hλ)| ≤ 1. Explicit methods have bounded regions; implicit ones (backward Euler) are stable for any step on decaying problems.
chapters.looks: The stability region in the complex hλ-plane with your hλ as a dot (2D); |R| as a surface with the unit level (3D).
chapters.change: Slide h up on a stiff problem: the dot leaves the region and the solution explodes.
chapters.use: Choosing solvers for chemical kinetics, circuits and structural dynamics (stiff systems).
misc: Accuracy and stability are different requirements.
A method can be stable and still inaccurate.

examples.title: Explicit Euler on a stiff decay
examples.world: λ = −20, h = 0.12: |R| = 1.4 — oscillating blow-up.

examples.title: Implicit Euler is unconditionally stable
examples.world: λ = −50, h = 0.5: |R| = 1/26, fine at any step.

examples.title: RK4 reaches further along the real axis
examples.world: hλ = −2.5 is stable for RK4 (|R| = 0.648) but not for Euler.

examples.title: Euler spirals out on an oscillator

examples.title: The trapezoid rule keeps oscillations exactly
examples.world: Crank–Nicolson: |R| = 1 on the imaginary axis.

examples.title: Energy drift of Euler on the harmonic oscillator
examples.world: The phase-plane circle becomes an outward spiral.

chapters.title: Numerical linear algebra
chapters.what: Large systems are solved by elimination (LU) or by iteration (Jacobi, Gauss–Seidel, SOR) that converges when the matrix is diagonally dominant; the condition number bounds how errors are amplified.
chapters.looks: Iterates zig-zagging toward the intersection of the lines (2D) or planes (3D).
chapters.change: Tune SOR's ω between 1 and 2: the number of iterations drops sharply near the optimum.
chapters.use: Finite-element and finite-difference solvers, circuit simulation, least squares.
misc: Gauss–Seidel is not always faster than Jacobi.
Never invert a matrix to solve a system.

examples.world: Roughly twice as fast as Jacobi here.

examples.world: The matrix of a 1D heat or Poisson problem; solution (1, 2, 3).

chapters.title: Numerical PDEs
chapters.what: Finite differences replace derivatives on a grid. Explicit schemes march in time under a stability limit (r ≤ ½ for heat, Courant ≤ 1 for waves); elliptic problems are solved by iteration.
chapters.looks: The solution profile marching (2D) and the whole space–time surface (3D).
chapters.change: Raise r past ½ and watch the checkerboard instability grow from round-off.
chapters.use: Heat treatment, acoustics, electrostatics, groundwater and weather models.
misc: Stability limits come from the scheme, not from the physics.
Refining the grid in space forces smaller time steps for explicit schemes.
